title: Food and eating out
objectives: Say what you like and dislike with gusto and ayaw + ng
Use the possessor-form (ng-form) pronouns: ko, mo, niya, namin, natin, ninyo, nila
Order food and drinks politely with pahingi po and isang... po
Talk about Filipino dishes and say something is delicious

grammar.title: The possessor-form pronouns (ng-form)
grammar.explanation:
Here is the second pronoun set, the one you've been seeing in chunks like kaibigan ko and gusto ko. Grammars call it the 'ng-form'; think of it as the possessor form. The set: ko (I/my), mo (you/your), niya (he/she, his/her), namin (our, not yours), natin (our, including yours), ninyo (your, plural or polite), nila (their).

Job one: possession. Put the pronoun AFTER the noun: kape ko (my coffee), bahay namin (our house), guro ninyo (your teacher). English says 'my coffee'; Tagalog says 'coffee my'.

Job two: the experiencer of gusto and ayaw, which you'll see in the next section: gusto ko, ayaw niya.

The kami/tayo split carries over: namin excludes the listener, natin includes them. So bahay namin = 'our house (not yours)', but kape natin = 'our coffee (yours and mine)'. And like ka, these words can never start a sentence — they always lean on the word before them.

examples.tl: Masarap ang adobo ng nanay ko.

grammar.title: Liking and disliking: gusto / ayaw + ng
grammar.explanation:
Gusto means 'like/want' and ayaw means 'dislike/don't want'. The pattern is: gusto + possessor pronoun + ng + thing. Gusto ko ng kape — 'I want/like coffee.' Ayaw niya ng gulay — 'He doesn't like vegetables.'

That little word ng (pronounced 'nang') is the second great marker of Tagalog, the partner of ang. It marks a noun that is NOT the topic — here, the thing liked. You've already met it inside litrato ng pamilya ko ('photo of my family'); with ordinary nouns it often translates as 'of' or 'a/some'.

To ask what someone wants: Ano ang gusto mo? — 'What do you like/want?' Polite, to a customer: Ano po ang gusto ninyo? To answer with just the thing: Gusto ko ng sinigang. To refuse: Ayaw ko po. (No ng needed when there's no noun.)

Careful: gusto does NOT take an ang-form pronoun. 'I like coffee' is gusto KO, never gusto AKO — gusto ako would mean someone likes you!

examples.tl: Gusto ko ng kape at tinapay.
Ano po ang gusto ninyo? — Gusto ko po ng sinigang.
examples.en: What would you like? — I'd like sinigang.

examples.tl: Gusto mo ba ng saging? — Ayaw ko, salamat.
examples.en: Would you like a banana? — No thanks.

grammar.title: Ordering politely: pahingi po ng..., isang... po
grammar.explanation:
In a carinderia or restaurant, the friendliest way to ask for something is pahingi po ng + thing: Pahingi po ng tubig — 'May I have some water, please.' Pahingi belongs to the same polite request family as paki- from Unit 2.

You can also just state quantity + item + po: Isang kape po at dalawang pandesal po — 'One coffee and two pandesal, please.' Remember the number linker from Unit 2: isang kape, dalawang itlog, tatlong saging.

To finish your order: Iyon lang po — 'That's all.' To praise the food: Masarap! or, with feeling, Ang sarap! — 'How delicious!' (Ang + the bare root turns an adjective into an exclamation.) And two states you'll feel daily: Gutom na ako ('I'm hungry now') and Uhaw pa ako ('I'm still thirsty').

examples.tl: Isang kape po at dalawang pandesal.
examples.en: One coffee and two pandesal, please.

vocab.note: Takes a possessor pronoun: gusto ko, gusto niya
Same pattern as gusto: ayaw ko, ayaw nila

example.tl: Ayaw ko ng gatas sa kape.
example.en: I don't like milk in my coffee.
This is our (your and my) bread.
May I have some water, please.

example.tl: May gatas ba ang kape na ito?
Gusto ko ng tinapay at kape.
Ayaw ng anak ko ng isda.
Gusto ko ng gulay sa ulam.
example.en: I like vegetables in the dish.

example.tl: Gusto ng pusa namin ng saging!

vocab.en: adobo (meat stewed in soy sauce and vinegar)

example.tl: Gusto ko ng sinigang na isda.
Isang kape po. Iyon lang po.

dialogue.title: At the carinderia
dialogue.context: Ana and Kate order lunch at a small eatery. Aling Nena runs it.

lines.speaker: Aling Nena
lines.tl: Magandang tanghali! Ano po ang gusto ninyo?
lines.en: Good noon! What would you like?

lines.speaker: Ana
lines.tl: Ano ang ulam ninyo ngayon po?

lines.speaker: Aling Nena
lines.tl: May adobo, sinigang na isda, at gulay po.
lines.en: We have adobo, fish sinigang, and vegetables.

lines.speaker: Ana
lines.tl: Gusto ko po ng adobo at kanin.

lines.speaker: Aling Nena
lines.tl: Ikaw, ineng? Ano ang sa iyo?
lines.en: And you, miss? What will you have?

lines.speaker: Kate
lines.tl: Ayaw ko po ng isda... Gusto ko po ng sinigang na manok. Mayroon po ba?
lines.en: I don't like fish... I'd like chicken sinigang. Do you have that?

lines.speaker: Aling Nena
lines.tl: Wala po ngayon. Pero masarap ang adobo namin!
lines.en: Not today. But our adobo is delicious!

lines.speaker: Kate
lines.tl: Sige po, adobo na rin. At pahingi po ng dalawang tubig.
lines.en: Alright, adobo as well then. And two waters, please.

lines.speaker: Aling Nena
lines.tl: May halo-halo rin po kami. Gusto ninyo ba?
lines.en: We also have halo-halo. Would you like some?

lines.speaker: Ana
lines.tl: Oo naman po! Dalawang halo-halo po. Iyon lang po.
lines.en: Of course! Two halo-halo, please. That's all.

lines.speaker: Kate
lines.tl: Mmm, ang sarap ng adobo ninyo, Aling Nena!
lines.en: Mmm, your adobo is so delicious, Aling Nena!

lines.speaker: Aling Nena
lines.en: Thank you very much! Eat some more!

exercises.prompt: Which is correct for 'I like coffee'?
exercises.explain: Gusto takes the possessor-form pronoun ko; gusto ako would mean someone likes YOU.

exercises.prompt: What does 'Ayaw niya ng gulay' mean?
exercises.explain: Ayaw is 'dislike/don't want', niya is 'he/she', and ng gulay marks vegetables as the thing disliked.
The thing wanted after gusto is marked with ng: gusto ko ng sinigang.

exercises.prompt: Masarap ang adobo ___ nanay ko. (My mom's adobo is delicious — 'adobo OF my mom')
exercises.explain: Ng links two nouns as 'of': adobo ng nanay ko = the adobo of my mom.

exercises.prompt: A waiter politely asks a table of customers what they want. Which is right?
exercises.explain: Ninyo is the plural/polite 'your', matching po; mo would be too casual for customers.

exercises.tl: Pahingi po ng dalawang pandesal at isang kape.
choices: Two coffees and one bread roll
Two bread rolls and one coffee
One bread roll and two waters
exercises.explain: Dalawang pandesal is two bread rolls and isang kape is one coffee; pahingi po ng makes it a polite request.

exercises.prompt: This is OUR house — yours and mine: Bahay ___ ito.
exercises.explain: Natin includes the person you're talking to; namin would exclude them.

exercises.prompt: I don't like fish. I like chicken.
exercises.answer: Ayaw ko ng isda. Gusto ko ng manok.
accept: Ayaw ko ng isda. Gusto ko ng manok
Ayaw ko po ng isda. Gusto ko po ng manok
Ayaw ko ng isda, gusto ko ng manok
exercises.explain: Both ayaw and gusto take ko + ng + the food: ayaw ko ng isda, gusto ko ng manok.

exercises.tl: Gutom na ako! Ano ang ulam natin?
choices: I'm thirsty — where is the water?
I'm hungry — what's our main dish?
I'm full — the food was delicious.
exercises.explain: Gutom na ako = 'I'm hungry now'; ulam is the main dish eaten with rice, and natin is 'our'.

exercises.prompt: Masarap ang pansit ni Tita Rosa, pero ayaw ng kuya ko ng gulay.
exercises.answer: Aunt Rosa's pancit is delicious, but my older brother doesn't like vegetables.
accept: Aunt Rosa's pancit is delicious, but my older brother doesn't like vegetables
Tita Rosa's pansit is delicious but my older brother does not like vegetables
Aunt Rosa's noodles are delicious, but my older brother doesn't like vegetables
exercises.explain: Ni marks the named owner (pansit ni Tita Rosa), and ayaw ng kuya ko ng gulay stacks two ng-phrases: the one who dislikes, and the thing disliked.

exercises.prompt: You've finished ordering. How do you say 'That's all, please'?
exercises.explain: Iyon lang po — literally 'just that' — is the set phrase for closing an order.

exercises.prompt: May I have some water, please. And one halo-halo. That's all.
exercises.answer: Pahingi po ng tubig. At isang halo-halo po. Iyon lang po.
accept: Pahingi po ng tubig. At isang halo-halo po. Iyon lang po
Pahingi po ng tubig at isang halo-halo. Iyon lang po
Pahingi po ng tubig. Isang halo-halo po. Iyon lang po
exercises.explain: Pahingi po ng + noun requests politely; isang halo-halo uses the number linker; iyon lang po closes the order.

exercises.prompt: Gusto mo ba ng kape? You want to refuse politely. Which reply is natural?
exercises.explain: Ayaw ko po refuses an offer (with the possessor ko, not ako); adding salamat keeps it friendly.
